reading.title: The Chalkboard Note
reading.purpose: Trace how one brief question on a school hallway board sparks a chain of real changes.
paras: On Monday morning, someone wrote a single question on the hallway chalkboard at Cedar Middle School: "Why do new students eat alone?" Nobody knew who started it, yet that short line was enough to trigger a wave of talk before first period even began.

At lunch, the note began to provoke strong reactions across the cafeteria. Some seventh-graders shrugged, saying seating charts were nobody's fault, while sixth-grader Keiko felt a twist of guilt. She realized her own table rarely invited anyone outside her homeroom.

The idea for an open-seating table seemed to originate right there between Keiko and her friend Sam. "One small gesture can have real influence," Sam said, reminding her that people notice when a group makes room. They asked Ms. Ortiz if they could place a bright green sign on Table Four.

By Thursday, the outcome surprised even the principal. Due to the simple welcome sign, twelve students from different grades shared lunch together and traded book recommendations. Everyone wanted to contribute a part, so art club members painted extra signs and eighth-graders offered to greet newcomers at the door.

Keiko had never expected one chalk sentence to leave such a lasting impact on the whole school. Fewer students hovered near the hallway doors, and thus the lunchroom grew louder with easy laughter. One honest question had opened a door; hence, Cedar Middle felt smaller and friendlier by Friday afternoon.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "contribute" most nearly means
choices: to complain loudly about an unfair cafeteria rule
to give a part toward a shared effort or goal
to ask the principal to cancel the hallway chalkboard
to erase a message before first period starts
qs.why: Paragraph 4 shows students contributing by painting extra signs and greeting newcomers so everyone gives a part.

qs.q: Which sentence shows the direct result of placing the welcome sign on Table Four?
choices: On Monday morning, someone wrote a single question on the hallway chalkboard at Cedar Middle School: "Why do new students eat alone?"
She realized her own table rarely invited anyone outside her homeroom.
Due to the simple welcome sign, twelve students from different grades shared lunch together and traded book recommendations.
Keiko had never expected one chalk sentence to leave such a lasting impact on the whole school.
qs.why: This sentence directly names what happened because of the welcome sign: twelve students from different grades ate together.

ev.text: Due to the simple welcome sign, twelve students from different grades shared lunch together and traded book recommendations.

qs.q: Why did Keiko feel a twist of guilt after reading the chalkboard note?
choices: She had accidentally broken the hallway chalk earlier that morning.
She had told the seventh-graders not to sit near any new students.
She knew Ms. Ortiz wanted her to paint extra signs for the art club.
She realized her own lunch group had not been welcoming.
qs.why: Paragraph 2 says Keiko realized her own table rarely invited anyone outside her homeroom.

qs.q: What is this story mostly about?
choices: One hallway question sets off small actions that make lunch friendlier.
An art club competes with eighth-graders to paint the brightest cafeteria sign.
A principal investigates who wrote an unsigned message on the school chalkboard.
Two sixth-graders struggle to find enough chairs for their homeroom friends.
qs.why: The story traces a chain of cause and effect from one chalkboard question to a welcoming lunchroom.
